lead: A program can go wrong in three different ways, and Python gives a different symptom for each. Bad grammar stops the file before a single line runs. A valid line that fails while running stops the program and prints a traceback. A program that runs to the end and prints the wrong number gives no message at all. Telling the three apart decides where you look: at the line's spelling, at the failing value, or at your own logic.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for names and keywords, 1.5 for types, and 1.7 for indentation, because you need working code before you can break it.

blocks.text: Python handles a file in two stages. First it reads the whole file and translates it into internal instructions. Only then does it run those instructions, one statement at a time, from top to bottom. Which stage fails decides which family of error you get.

items: Syntax error. The grammar is wrong. Nothing in the file runs, not even the correct lines above the mistake.
Runtime error. The grammar is fine, but a statement cannot be carried out with the values it meets. Python stops at that statement.
Semantic error, also called a logic error. Every statement runs, the program ends normally, and the output is wrong. No message appears anywhere.

blocks.text: Python's built-in error names end in Error: ZeroDivisionError, NameError, TypeError, ValueError. Catching them on purpose is Unit 5. Here you only need to read them.
Syntax means grammar: where the brackets, colons, quotes and keywords go. A syntax error means Python could not parse the line at all. Usual causes:

items: A missing colon after if x > 0, for i in range(3) or def f().
A misspelled keyword: fro i in range(3):. Keywords are fixed words, listed in 1.4.

blocks.text: Python prints SyntaxError, the file name, the line number, and a caret ^ under the place where parsing stopped. Then it stops. The caret marks the first point where the line stopped making sense, which for a missing bracket is often later than the real mistake. Two relatives are also syntax errors: IndentationError for wrong spacing at the start of a line, and TabError when one block mixes tabs and spaces. Both are subclasses of SyntaxError, so both stop the whole file before any statement runs. The indentation rules are in 1.7.

A runtime error is a statement that is legal Python but fails on the actual values. Python prints the error name, then a traceback: the file, the line number, and the chain of calls that led there. The four you meet first:

items: NameError: the name does not exist, for example print(total) when the variable is spelled totl.
TypeError: the type forbids the operation, for example "Age: " + 25, which adds a str to an int. Convert one side first, see 1.5.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not acceptable, for example int("abc") or int("12.5").

blocks.text: Read a traceback from the bottom up. The last line is the error name and its message. The line just above is the file and line number where it happened. Everything above that is the call chain. Beginners start at the top, meet an unfamiliar function name from inside Python's own code, and give up. Work from the bottom. Python stops at the first runtime error, so fixing one may reveal a second.

sections.h3: Semantic errors and a debugging routine

blocks.text: The hardest family has no message. The program computes something, prints it, and the number is wrong. Debugging is the routine that finds it.

items: Reproduce with the smallest input you can: 10 and 20, not a 500-row file.
Read the traceback bottom-up, or if there is none, note the line that prints the wrong value.
Print the intermediate values just before that line.
Compare each printed value with what you expected. The first one that differs contains the bug.
Fix one thing, run again, and delete the debug prints.

blocks.code:
def average(a, b):
    print("a =", a, "b =", b)
    return a + b / 2

result = average(10, 20)
print("result =", result)

blocks.text: The prints show the inputs arrived correctly, so the bug is inside the calculation: / binds tighter than + (see 1.6), so it computed 10 + 10.0. The corrected line return (a + b) / 2 gives 15.0. Most semantic errors are one of four things: operator precedence, integer division where you wanted /, a variable never updated inside a loop (Unit 2), or an off-by-one in a range.

figure.caption: The file is read whole before any statement runs, so bad grammar stops everything at once; a crash stops a valid run partway; a wrong result passes through silently.

spec.title: Which error, when
spec.aria: A decision flow: the file is read whole, bad syntax stops it at once, a crash stops it mid-run, and a wrong result runs to the end with no message.

examples.question: A student must print the average of 10 and 20, which is 15.0. Four attempts follow. Classify each one and state exactly what Python does with it. (a) print(10 + 20 / 2) (b) print(10 / 2 + missing) (c) print((10 + 20) / 2 (d) print(10 / 0)
steps: (a) Parses correctly. / binds tighter than +, so 20 / 2 = 10.0, then 10 + 10.0 = 20.0. The program ends normally and prints 20.0, not 15.0. No message appears. Semantic error.
(b) Parses correctly. Python evaluates 10 / 2 = 5.0, then looks up the name missing. No such name exists, so it raises NameError and stops at that line. Runtime error.
(c) Has two opening brackets and only one closing bracket. Python cannot parse the file, reports SyntaxError for that line, and runs nothing at all. No output. Syntax error.
(d) Parses correctly. 10 / 0 has no value, so Python raises ZeroDivisionError: division by zero and stops. Runtime error.
The corrected line is print((10 + 20) / 2), which prints 15.0.
examples.answer: One syntax error at (c), two runtime errors at (b) and (d), and one semantic error at (a); the corrected line prints 15.0.

examples.question: What does this program print, and which statement would break it? x = "5", print(int(x) + 5).
steps: int("5") converts the string to the integer 5. The type is correct and the value is valid, so no error.
Replace it with print(x + 5) and Python raises TypeError at runtime: it cannot add str and int.
examples.answer: The program prints 10; without the conversion it would stop with a TypeError.

traps: A misspelled function name, prnt("hi"), is a NameError at runtime, not a syntax error. The grammar is perfect.
The reported SyntaxError line is where parsing gave up, not always where the bug is. For an unbalanced bracket, look at the lines above.
int("12.5") raises ValueError, not TypeError and not a syntax error: the type is right, the value is not.
IndentationError and TabError look like runtime problems but stop the file before any statement runs, exactly like SyntaxError.
No message does not mean no bug. A program that prints 20.0 when the answer is 15.0 ran to the end and is still wrong.

quiz.q: Name the three error families and say which one prints no message.
quiz.a: Syntax error (nothing runs), runtime error (stops mid-run with a traceback), and semantic or logic error (runs to the end, wrong output, no message).

quiz.q: Which error is raised when one indentation block mixes tabs and spaces, and is it a syntax error?
quiz.a: TabError. Yes, it is a subclass of SyntaxError, so the whole file stops before any statement runs.

quiz.q: Why does a SyntaxError prevent even the correct lines above it from running?
quiz.a: Python reads and translates the entire file before executing any statement. A parse failure stops that first stage, so execution never begins.
(i) runs correctly and prints 3.0. (ii) ZeroDivisionError at runtime. (iii) TypeError at runtime, str + int. (iv) ValueError at runtime, the string is not a whole number.

quiz.q: A file has print("Total: " + 25) on line 4 and a missing colon on line 7. What does the student see?
quiz.a: Only the SyntaxError for line 7. The file never runs, so the TypeError on line 4 is never reached. Fix line 7 first, then the runtime error appears.

quiz.q: A program that averages ten marks prints 0 for every input, with no message. Which family is this, and what two checks do you make first?
quiz.a: Semantic error. First, print the running sum just before the division to see whether it is being updated. Second, check whether the division uses the count correctly and is not doing integer division on a mis-set variable.

quiz.q: A traceback shows the student's line at the top and a Python library function at the bottom. Which line should be read first, and why?
quiz.a: The bottom line. It gives the error name and message, and the line above it gives the exact file and line number where the failure happened. The top of the traceback is only the call chain.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real projects do not trust the eye: linters such as pylint, flake8 and ruff flag likely bugs before the program runs, and type checkers such as mypy catch int-plus-str mistakes without executing anything. Python ships a debugger, pdb, which pauses a running program so you can inspect variables instead of printing them. The logging module writes messages with timestamps and severity levels, so they can stay in production code. Search for 'Python pdb tutorial', 'ruff linter' or 'Python logging basics' to go further.
